name: Square Boucicaut
short_description: Public square in the 7th arrondissement commemorating Aristide and Marguerite Boucicaut, founders of Le Bon Marché, with a sculpture of Madame Boucicaut at its entrance.

beats.script_body: Square Boucicaut commemorates Aristide Boucicaut, the founder of the Bon Marché department store across the street, which he opened in 1852, and his wife and business partner, Marguerite Guerin Boucicaut. When Aristide died, Marguerite inherited his fortune — one of the largest in nineteenth-century Paris — and gave most of it away: to poor children, to hospitals, teachers, journalists, and artists. The sculpture of Madame Boucicaut at the square's entrance captures the kindliness of the woman, an exceptionally generous Parisian who began life as the illegitimate daughter of a peasant.

beats.script_body: The Austrian journalist Joseph Roth, described by Jeffrey Eugenides as "non-stop brilliant," wrote of the children of Paris in his essay "The Child in Paris": "There are children playing in all the parks. . . . French children behave with the ease and confidence of grown-ups. It's not so much a matter of race and blood as it is the consequence of the warm, loving, nurturing softness in the way they are brought up. The French pedagogical principle is not Spartan strictness but Roman freedom accorded to the individual disposition — it's not discipline but civilisation." Looking at the Madame Boucicaut monument in the context of this Austrian's take on Parisian child-rearing, the writer notes, strikes a major chord of recognition.

beats.script_body: In the spirit of French contrariness, the nineteenth-century poet Charles Baudelaire, who felt a brotherhood with the Paris of the poor, might have felt only dislike toward this stone homage to the tradition of philanthropy. Eric Hazan notes that in Les Fleurs du Mal, Baudelaire "never shows pity for the poor, nor — still worse — charitable tenderness, sentiments so widespread at the time, and that drove him into a rage."

name: Jardin de la Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu
short_description: Hidden rose garden behind the Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu hospital at 19 rue Oudinot, accessible during visiting hours; one of the finest rose gardens in Paris.

beats.poi_name: Jardin de la Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu
beats.script_body: A pleasant receptionist in the hospital lobby at 19, rue Oudinot will guide you down a short hallway and through doors to the left. If you visit in May and June, what awaits you outside, behind the hospital, is one of the most beautiful rose gardens in Paris. The garden of Saint-Jean de Dieu (Saint John of God) feels like a state of being — not a performance like the Bagatelle in the Bois du Boulogne. Sitting far in the back, facing the fine white building that was originally the town house of Madame de la Sablière, the long view of manicured flower beds beneath sheltering trees can make you feel as if you've come into an outdoor church sanctuary. The occasional crunch of pebbles on a path as a visiting friend and a patient stroll past arm-in-arm is all you hear. To your right are the high old rooftops of rue Rousselet, alongside the clinic garden, admired for its quiet charm.

beats.poi_name: Jardin de la Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu
beats.script_body: The healing spirituality of the hospital garden is now a theme among medical professionals who advocate making such green spaces integral parts of medical facilities. A garden, it is said, reaches a deeper level of being than the simply visual: it holds a "reservoir of feelings, such as pleasure, displeasure, awe, fear, or fascination" with the power "to heal psychic stress." Vegetation serves as a shock absorber for the human sensory system assaulted by the sights, smells, and sounds of the city. It does not present a challenge to the senses but provides an opportunity for rest from the constant mental alertness, helping to heal the psychological wounds congested cities inflict on their residents.

beats.poi_name: Jardin de la Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu
beats.script_body: The hospital was founded by a member of the Order of Saint John of God in 1843 — a fraternity that opened hospitals to serve the poor and the sick in Spain and France in 1546. Disbanded during the Terror, the Order reestablished itself in nineteenth-century Paris. Saint-Jean de Dieu, named for the founder, is no longer run by a religious community serving the poor. It is now a private operation serving the comfortable environs of le septième.

name: Musee Rodin
short_description: Sculpture museum in the 18th-century Hotel Biron with The Thinker and The Gates of Hell displayed in a formal garden

beats.script_body: The spacious gardens of the Musée Rodin can be visited independently of the museum — the most popular in Paris dedicated to a single artist. In Rodin's day, this was a wild park. A makeover in 1993 established a highly designed layout well suited to the architecture of the museum, an elegant eighteenth-century mansion. A variety of trees — lindens, chestnuts, trimmed box trees, clipped yews — complement the generous flower beds and a large pool. The entire composition frames the mansion's south façade, where Rodin (1840–1917) had his studio. The trees you can see from his studio windows, he wrote in Cathedrals of France, would have delighted him: "Trees bring order and animation to everything . . . like archangels, [they] bow their heads to one another, their wings unfurled vertical against the sky."

beats.script_body: The most powerful presences in the garden are the sculptures, scattered about in the open, others discreetly set among holly bushes and other greenery. Along one path, thick with plantings, you suddenly come upon The Thinker — and all the thinking tourists posing for cameras in front of him. Elsewhere are The Burghers of Calais; The Gates of Hell, influenced by the imagery of Dante's Divine Comedy and Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel; and in the pool, Ugolino and His Children. Inside the museum are sketches and models Rodin made for his masterpiece, the Honoré de Balzac monument. There's a copy in the garden; the original, which Parisians despised at first, stands on a pedestal under trees on a median at the intersection of boulevard du Montparnasse and boulevard Raspail in Montparnasse.

beats.script_body: In late afternoon, as the sun fades slowly in the west behind the nearby gold dome of Les Invalides and the Eiffel Tower seems to touch the pink sky, the gardens feel animated by the spirit of the artists who had their studios in the mansion with Rodin — as well as by the city that at once inspired and enraged them. One of the artists who shared his space was the sculptor Camille Claudel (1864–1943), Rodin's collaborator and lover for eleven years. Their breakup, like their affair, was tempestuous, having lifelong tragic consequences for Claudel.

beats.script_body: It was Rodin's friend, the poet Rainer Maria Rilke (1875–1926), who first told him about the available studio space in what was then called Hôtel Biron, and who later worked as his office assistant. Rilke's novel The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, completed after his first stay in Paris in 1908, tells the story of his survival in those early years in the alienating yet supremely alive city. After Rodin's death, Rilke wrote a brilliant monograph about his friend. His insights, contemplated in the silence of this garden in late afternoon, achieve a rich texture: "Indeed, it is an underlying patience in Rodin which renders him so great, a silent, superior forbearance resembling the wonderful patience and kindness of Nature. . . . 'One must not hurry,' said Rodin. . . . He possessed the quiet perseverance of men who are necessary."

flagged_claims.notes: Research indicates it was Clara Rilke (Rainer Maria's wife) who discovered the Hôtel Biron in 1907 and told Rilke, who then told Rodin. The Musée Rodin's own website confirms: 'in 1908, the two men reconciled at the Hôtel Biron, which Clara Rilke had discovered the previous year.' Rilke did move there and suggested it to Rodin — so Rilke's role in alerting Rodin is broadly confirmed, but the book simplifies by omitting Clara's prior discovery. Not auto-corrected (complex attribution; source says 'Rilke first told him' and the truth is 'Rilke and Clara together led Rodin to the space'). Sources: https://www.musee-rodin.fr/en/resources/rodin-life/houses-and-workshops/hotel-biron ; http://writersinpariswalkingtours.blogspot.com/2016/04/rilke-and-rodin-how-musee-rodin-came.html

name: Le Bon Marché
short_description: The world's first modern department store, founded 1838 at 24 rue de Sèvres; inspiration for Zola's Au Bonheur des Dames.

beats.script_body: Partly designed by Gustave Eiffel in a brilliant glass-and-steel construction like London's Crystal Palace, Le Bon Marché is as much a light-filled, welcoming museum as a department store — the oldest in Paris.

name: Hotel Lutetia
short_description: Historic Left Bank luxury hotel at 45 boulevard Raspail, requisitioned by German forces during the Occupation and used as a repatriation centre for POWs and concentration camp survivors after the Liberation.

beats.script_body: The Hôtel Lutetia at 45 boulevard Raspail, opposite Square Boucicaut, was a destination for artists and writers — Henry James, Matisse, and Picasso all chose to stay here. During the Occupation, the Nazis installed the Gestapo here. After the Liberation, Paris received its returning POWs and concentration camp survivors here. In her book La Douleur, writer and Résistante Marguerite Duras (1914–1996) caught the sorrow and the muted relief of the days of repatriation. A plaque, in French, bears witness to the Lutetia's tragic role during World War II.

During the Occupation, the Naps installed the Gestapo; after the Liberation, Paris received its returning POIVs and concentration camp survivors here. flagged_claims.notes: Multiple sources indicate the Lutetia was requisitioned by the Abwehr (German military counter-intelligence), not the Gestapo proper. Do NOT auto-correct (requires story-level rewrite, not a simple substitution). Flag for editorial review.
flagged_claims.recommendation: Flag for user review — simplification vs. factual error; change to 'Abwehr' (German military intelligence) or leave as book's framing with note.

visit_basis: Ornate Art Nouveau hotel facade with a memorial plaque worth about 12 min outside; the public lobby and bar can be stepped into for roughly 15 min, but it is a working hotel not a visitor site.
judgement_basis: This is a luxury hotel fronting the busy boulevard Raspail with no traffic-free running ground and no free public seating, but the boulevard is well lit and trafficked into the night so someone could safely be left standing outside it.
queue_basis: A working luxury hotel walked past or entered through its lobby doors with no admission line or screening, so there is no queue to price.

name: Jardin Catherine-Laboure
short_description: Vegetable and flower garden on the grounds of the Sisters of Charity convent at 33 rue de Babylone, with an arbor; a haven for Parisians at lunchtime.

beats.script_body: At 33, rue de Babylone is the Jardin Catherine-Laboure — a tidy vegetable and flower garden on the grounds of the Sisters of Charity convent, with a lovely arbor. A haven for Parisians at lunchtime, just a few minutes' walk from Square Boucicaut.

fact_check.notes: Garden confirmed at 33 rue de Babylone on grounds of the Daughters of Charity (Sisters of Charity) convent — Wikipedia confirms location and convent connection: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jardin_Catherine-Labour%C3%A9

opening_hours_basis: A walled convent garden with closing gates; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Walled convent garden with vegetable plots, flower beds, lawns and a vine-covered arbor; strolling and sitting absorbs around 18 min, all outdoors.
judgement_basis: This walled convent garden is fully enclosed and traffic-free with lawns and an arbor where children can run and quiet benches for lunchtime conversation, but as a gated garden on convent grounds it is locked at night.
queue_basis: A convent-grounds public garden on rue de Babylone entered freely through an open gate with no ticket or bag check, so there is no queue.

name: Eglise Sainte-Clotilde
short_description: 19th-century neo-Gothic church in the 7th arrondissement, built by architects Gau and Ballu; famous as the church where César Franck served as organist for over 30 years.

beats.script_body: The Basilica of Saint-Clotilde at 25, rue las Casas is a lovely nineteenth-century mock Gothic cathedral where César Franck was the organist for fifty years — and now the setting for glorious choral concerts featuring Brahms, Mendelssohn, Bach, and Fauré. Edith Wharton, who lived nearby at 53, rue de Varenne, loved the sound of Saint-Clotilde's church bells.

beats.source_passage: BASILICA OF SAINT-CLOTILDE 2j, rue las Casas. Metro, Solferino. A lovely nineteenth-century mock Gothic cathedral, where Cesar Franck was the organist for fifty years, and now the setting for glorious choral concerts (Brahms, Mendelssohn, Bach, Faure). Schedules available at www.sainte-clotilde.com. Edith Wharton, who lived nearby at ,5j, rue de Varenne, loved the sound of Saint-Clotilde's church bells.

fact_check.notes: Eglise Sainte-Clotilde is an existing POI; César Franck as organist for fifty years confirmed in prior extraction (beat: eglise_sainte_clotilde_music_heritage_cesar_franck_organist_around_and_about_paris). Edith Wharton's address at 53 rue de Varenne is well documented. Note: OCR garbled the address digits ('2j' and ',5j') — cross-referencing known records, the church is at 23 bis rue Las Cases and Wharton at 53 rue de Varenne.

opening_hours_basis: A church you enter; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: 19th-century neo-Gothic church with twin spires on a garden square; interior has a tall nave, stained glass and the organ associated with César Franck, about 18 minutes to see.
judgement_basis: A church interior demands quiet so children cannot run, and its surrounding square has no reliable free seating, but the adjacent square is lit and set on trafficked residential streets after dark.
queue_basis: A neo-Gothic parish church with an open door and free entry; visitors walk straight in without a ticket or screening.
